claims.text: As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure.
The proposed framework integrates reduced-order finite-element outputs with image-derived hierarchical microstructural descriptors.
The proposed framework will predict the properties of HfNbTiVAl10 faster than conventional single-scale simulations.
The proposed framework will predict Young's modulus and yield strength more accurately than conventional single-scale simulations.
The proposed framework will predict fracture-related behavior more accurately than conventional single-scale simulations.
The hierarchical microstructure remains stable during room-temperature to moderate-loading tensile and fracture testing.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates interactions between micro- and meso-scale features that influence elasticity, yielding, crack initiation, and crack propagation.
Combining physics-based outputs with microstructural descriptors enables the model to capture interfacial effects and heterogeneous interactions governing mechanical response.
The framework will reduce computational time by roughly one order of magnitude.
The framework will reduce prediction errors for Young's modulus and yield strength by more than 50%.
Predicted Young's modulus and yield strength will be within 15% of independent experimental measurements.
Conventional finite-element and atomistic baselines use homogenized or single-scale representations and require extensive computational resources.
Conventional simulation baselines have larger predictive errors than the proposed framework.
The approach may fail when substantial microstructural evolution makes the selected descriptors cease to represent active heterogeneities.
Surrogate-model accuracy and efficiency depend on dataset quality, feature selection, and the machine-learning algorithm.
Young's modulus can be measured from the elastic region of a stress-strain curve.
Yield strength can be determined by the 0.2% offset method.
Fracture toughness or crack-propagation resistance will be obtained from standardized fracture tests.
The hypothesis is falsified if any independently measured Young's modulus, yield strength, or fracture toughness differs from its model prediction by more than 15%.
